source_text: Iam nunc, ut et cetera compendio absoluam, quaecumque adhuc ut pusilla et infirma et indigna colligitis ad destructionem creatoris, simplici et certa ratione proponam: deum non potuisse humanos congressus inire, nisi humanos et sensus et adfectus suscepisset, per quos uim maiestatis suae, intolerabilem utique humanae mediocritati, humilitate temperaret. I sibi quidem indigna, homini autem necessaria, et ita iam deo digna, quia nihil tam dignum deo quam salus hominis. de isto pluribus retractarem, si cum ethnicis agerem, — quamquam et cum haereticis non multo diuersa congressio — sed quatenus et ipsi deum in figura et in reliquo ordine humanae condicionis deuersatum iam credidistis, non exigetis utique diutius persuaderi deum conformasse semetipsum humanitati, sed de uestra fide reuincimini. si enim deus, et quidem sublimior, tanta humilitate fastigium maiestatis suae strauit, ut etiam morti subiceretur, et morti crucis, cur non putetis nostro quoque deo aliquas pusillitates congruisse, tolerabiliores tamen ludaicis contumeliis et patibulis et sepulcris? an hae sunt pusillitates, quae iam hinc praeiudicare debebunt Christum humanis passionibus obiectum eius dei esse, cui humanitates exprobrantur a uobis? nam et profitemur Christum semper egisse in dei patris nomine, ipsum ab initio conuersatum, ipsum congressum cum patriarchis et prophetis, filium creatoris, sermonem eius, quem ex semetipso proferendo filium fecit et exinde omni dispositioni suae uoluntatique praefecit, diminuens illum modico citra angelos, sicut apud eum scriptum est. qua diminutione in haec quoque dispositus est a patre, quae ut humana reprehenditis, ediscens iam inde a primordio [iam inde hominem] quod erat futurus in fine. ille est, qui descendit, ille, qui interrogat, ille, qui postulat, ille, qui iurat. ceterum quia patrem nemini uisum etiam commune testabitur euangelium, dicente Christo: nemo cognouit patrem nisi filius. ipse enim et ueteri testamento pronuntiarat: deum nemo uidebit et uiuet, patrem inuisibilem determinans, in cuius auctoritate et nomine ipse erat deus, qui uidebatur dei filius. sed et penes nos Christus in persona Christi accipitur, quia et hoc modo noster est. igitur quaecumque exigitis deo digna, habe- Ii buntur in patre inuisibili incongressibilique et placido et, ut ita dixerim, philosophorum deo, quaecumque autem ut indigna reprehenditis, deputabuntur in filio et uiso et audito et congresso, arbitro patris et ministro, miscente in semetipso hominem et deum, in uirtutibus deum, in pusillitatibus hominem, ut tantum homini conferat quantum deo detrahit. totum denique\' dei mei penes uos dedecus sacramentum est humanae salutis. conuersabatur deus (humane,) ut homo diuine agere doceretur. ex aequo agebat deus cum homine, ut homo ex aequo agere cum deo posset. deus pusillus inuentus est, ut homo maximus fieret. qui talem deum dedignaris, nescie, an ex fide credas deum crucifixum. quanta itaque peruersitas uestra erga utrumque ordinem creatoris? iudicem eum desi-, gnatis, et seueritatem iudicis secundum merita causarum congruentem pro saeuitia exprobratis; deum optimum exigitis. et lenitatem eius benignitati congruentem, pro captu mediocritatis humanae deiectius conuersatam, ut pusillitatem depretiatis. nec magnus uobis placet nec modicus, nec iudex nec amicus. quid, si nunc eadem et in uestro deprehendantur? iudicem quidem et illum esse iam ostendimus in libello suo et de iudice necessarie seuerum et de seuero scilicet saeuum, si tamen saeuum.
pass_a_gloss: Now, so that I may also briefly settle the remaining matters, whatever small and weak and unworthy things you collect for the destruction of the creator, I will propose with a simple and certain reason: God was not able to enter into human interactions, unless He had also taken on human senses and affections, through which He might temper the force of His majesty, which is certainly intolerable to human mediocrity, with humility. These things are indeed unworthy of God, but necessary for man, and thus already worthy of God, because nothing is as worthy of God as the salvation of man. I would discuss this at greater length if I were dealing with pagans, — although the interaction is not much different even with heretics — but insofar as you also believe that God has already walked among men in the form and in the rest of the order of human condition, you will not require to be persuaded for a longer time that God conformed Himself to humanity, but you will be convinced by your own faith. For if God, and indeed the more exalted One, has cast down the height of His majesty with such great humility, that He even subjected Himself to death, and to the death of the cross, why do you not think that some smallnesses were fitting for our God as well, which are more tolerable than the Jewish insults and crosses and graves? Or are these smallnesses, which from now on ought to prejudice Christ, who was subjected to human passions, to be the God to whom human weaknesses are reproached by you? For we also confess that Christ always acted in the name of God the Father, that He was conversing with the patriarchs and prophets from the beginning, the Son of the creator, the Word of God, which He brought forth from Himself and made His Son, and from then on He placed Him over all His disposition and will, diminishing Him slightly below the angels, as it is written. By this diminution, He was also disposed by the Father to these things, which you reprehend as human, learning already from the beginning what He would be in the end. He is the One who descended, He is the One who asked, He is the One who requested, He is the One who swore. Moreover, because the Father has not been seen by anyone, even the common Gospel will testify, with Christ saying: No one has known the Father except the Son. For He had also declared in the Old Testament: No one will see God and live, determining the invisible Father, in whose authority and name He Himself was God, who was seen as the Son of God. But also among us, Christ is accepted in the person of Christ, because He is also ours in this way. Therefore, whatever things you require as worthy of God, will be found in the invisible and incongressible and peaceful Father, and, as I might say, the God of the philosophers, but whatever things you reprehend as unworthy, will be attributed to the Son, who was seen and heard and interacted with, the arbiter and minister of the Father, mixing in Himself man and God, God in virtues, man in smallnesses, so that He might confer on man as much as He detracts from God. Finally, the whole shame of my God, in your opinion, is the sacrament of human salvation. God was conversing with men, so that man might be taught to act divinely. God was acting equally with man, so that man might be able to act equally with God. God was found to be small, so that man might become great. You who disdain such a God, do not know whether you believe in a God who was crucified from faith. How great, therefore, is your perversity towards both orders of the creator? You despise Him as a judge, and you reprehend the severity of the judge, which is congruent with the merits of the causes, as savagery; you demand a most excellent God. And you convert the leniency of His benignity, which is congruent with the capacity of human mediocrity, into something worthless, so that you might depreciate the smallness. Neither the great nor the moderate pleases you, neither the judge nor the friend. What if the same things are now detected in your own God? We have already shown that He is a judge in His own book, and that the judge is necessarily severe, and that the severe one is certainly savage, if indeed He is savage.

pass_b_english: I will now settle the rest briefly. You gather up whatever petty, weak, and unworthy details you can find to tear down the Creator, but a simple, certain reason answers them all: God could not enter human life unless He took on human senses and affections, through which He could temper the force of His majesty — force utterly intolerable to human mediocrity — with humility. Such things are unworthy of God in themselves, yet necessary for man; that makes them worthy of God after all, because nothing is more worthy of God than human salvation. I would argue this at length if I were debating pagans — though the dispute with heretics is not much different — but since you already believe that God has walked among men in the form and full order of the human condition, your own faith should convince you that God conformed Himself to humanity. For if God, the more exalted One, has cast down the height of His majesty with such humility that He submitted even to death, and to death on a cross, why do you not think that some smallnesses were fitting for our God as well — smallnesses far more tolerable than the Jewish insults, crosses, and graves? Are these the smallnesses that should now prejudice Christ, subjected to human passions, into being the very God whose human weaknesses you reproach? We also confess that Christ always acted in the name of God the Father; He was conversing with the patriarchs and prophets from the beginning. He is the Son of the Creator, the Word of God, whom the Father brought forth from Himself and made His Son, placing Him over all His disposition and will, diminishing Him slightly below the angels, as it is written (Psalm 8:5; Hebrews 2:7). By this diminution the Father also appointed Him to the very things you condemn as merely human, learning already from the beginning what He would be in the end. He is the One who descended, the One who asked, the One who demanded, the One who swore. Moreover, because the Father has never been seen by anyone, the common Gospel itself testifies, with Christ saying: "No one has known the Father except the Son" (John 1:18; Matthew 11:27). For He had also declared in the Old Testament: "No one will see God and live" (Exodus 33:20), defining the invisible Father, in whose authority and name He Himself was the God who was seen as the Son of God. Among us, too, Christ is accepted in the person of Christ, because He is ours in that very way. Therefore, whatever you demand as worthy of God will be found in the invisible, unapproachable, peaceful Father — the philosophers' God, so to speak — but whatever you condemn as unworthy will be attributed to the Son, the One seen and heard and interacted with, the Father's arbiter and minister, blending in Himself man and God: God in virtues, man in smallnesses, so that He confers on man exactly as much as He detracts from God. Finally, the whole shame of my God, in your eyes, is the sacrament of human salvation. God conversed with men so that man might learn to act divinely. God acted on equal terms with man so that man might be able to act on equal terms with God. God was found small so that man might become great. You who disdain such a God do not know whether you believe in a crucified God by faith. How great, then, is your perversity toward both orders of the Creator? You despise Him as a judge, and you reproach the severity of the judge — severity congruent with the merits of the cases — as savagery; you demand a most excellent God. And you turn the leniency of His benignity — leniency congruent with the capacity of human mediocrity — into something worthless, so that you may depreciate the smallness. Neither the great nor the moderate pleases you, neither the judge nor the friend. What if the same things are now detected in your own God? We have already shown that He is a judge in His own book, and that a judge is necessarily severe, and that the severe one is certainly savage, if indeed He is savage.
